section_1.title: The Problem: Average vs. Instantaneous
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of 'average speed' (total distance/total time). Explain that while we can measure average speed over an interval, life happens in an instant. Set the stage for why we need a new mathematical tool to capture speed at a single, frozen moment.
section_1.example: A cheetah chasing a gazelle: We know its average speed over 10 seconds, but how fast is it moving at exactly the 3-second mark?

section_2.title: Visualizing the Slope: The Secant Line
section_2.content: Introduce a position-time graph. Show a secant line connecting two points on a curve. Explain that the slope of this line represents the average rate of change. Use an animation of one point sliding closer to the other to visually demonstrate the interval shrinking.
section_2.example: A position-time curve of a rocket launch. Drawing a straight line through two points on the curve shows average velocity between those two times.

section_3.title: The Limit: Shrinking the Interval
section_3.content: Define the 'Limit' concept: As the time interval approaches zero, the secant line morphs into a tangent line. Emphasize that the slope of this tangent line is the instantaneous rate of change.
section_3.example: An animation showing the secant line rotating and flattening as the two points merge into one point, finally becoming a single tangent line at the 3-second mark.

section_4.title: Defining the Derivative
section_4.content: Formalize the concept. Present the derivative formula: f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h. Connect the symbols back to the 'rise over run' concept, explaining that h is the tiny 'time gap' being squashed to zero.
section_4.example: Display the mathematical formula overlaying the graphical tangent line to show that the 'limit' is simply the precise calculation of that slope.

section_5.title: Summary and Real-world Application
section_5.content: Conclude by unifying the graphical (slope of tangent) and algebraic (the limit) perspectives. Explain that the derivative is the universal tool for measuring how things change at any precise instant.
section_5.example: Showing a speedometer in a self-driving car: The computer calculates the derivative of the position function thousands of times per second to provide the exact instantaneous speed.
